lay_term: Cardiokymography (CKG) is a procedure using a device that monitors the heart’s electrical activity and can alert the provider to abnormalities in the heart’s functioning.ExplanationA cardiokymography is a painless, noninvasive test that a provider does in his office or at another facility, for example, a hospital or clinic. The test is relatively short, normally five to 10 minutes, and is most beneficial when a provider performs it in conjunction with an exercise stress test. Providers can determine abnormalities in the left coronary artery by observing left ventricle motion in the heart. The patient lies on a bed or table. A technician attaches multiple electrodes to clean and, if necessary, shaved arms, legs, and chest. The patient should remain still, breathe normally, and avoid talking. Sometimes the technician might ask the patient to hold her breath momentarily. The electrical impulses of the heart translate onto paper as peaks and valleys which a provider interprets.TerminologyCoronary artery: Vessels that supply blood to the heart muscle, including the right or left coronary artery, left anterior descending, posterior descending, and circumflex. Electrode: A device that can transmit and receive electrical impulses; often connected to an insulated wire lead; providers may refer to leads as wires or electrodes or make reference to an electrode at the end of a lead. Ventricle of the heart: One of the two lower chambers in the human heart that receive blood from a corresponding upper chamber, or atrium, and from which blood is forced into the arteries.TipsSee also codes 93000 to 93042 for other cardiography procedures. If you are reporting only the professional component for the service, you should append professional component modifier 26 to the code. If you are reporting only the technical component for the service, you should append technical component modifier TC to the code unless the hospital provided the technical component. In that case, do not append modifier TC because the hospital’s portion is inherently technical. Do not append a professional or technical modifier to the code when reporting a global service in which one provider renders both the professional and technical components.Additional InfoUse Q codes for supplies, such as drugs, biologicals, and medical equipment, as well as services. Q codes represent supplies and services that do not have permanent codes in other sections of HCPCS. Read Less

short_description: Infusion therapy, using other than chemotherapeutic drugs, per visit
lay_term: This code reports infusion therapy, which is the administration of medication through a needle or catheter. This occurs when oral medication has become ineffective in treating a condition. This code does not include medications given for chemotherapy.ExplanationThe provider sterilizes the area where she will insert the needle. She then inserts the needle using access to a blood vessel, indwelling intravenous line, subcutaneous catheter, or port. Infusion devices can include cannulas, which are thin tubes that enter a vein through the skin; a drip, which uses a pump that pushes the drug into the vein at a constant rate; a central line, which is a thin tube that enters the body in the chest and ends at a large vein in the collarbone area; a peripherally inserted central catheter, or PICC line, which is a tube inserted into a vein in the upper arm and ends at a large vein near the heart; or an implantable port or Port–a–Cath®, which is a flexible plastic tube entering the skin of the chest or arm, under which is a thin rubber disk to allow repeated needle puncture. The provider then infuses medication into the patient intravenously. The provider removes the infusion needle at the end of the session. Report this code once per visit. Providers treat many types of conditions using infusion drug therapy other than chemotherapy. Providers infuse medications for conditions requiring antibiotic and antiviral intervention, hydration therapy, and parenteral nutrition. Providers give specialty infusions to patients needing blood factors, corticosteroids, or growth hormones. Some diseases for which providers may use infusion drug therapies include cancer, congestive heart failure, hemophilia, rheumatoid arthritis, multiple sclerosis, gastrointestinal disorders, and urinary tract infections.TerminologyBlood factors: Various components in plasma that facilitate blood clotting. Congestive heart failure: A condition in which excessive fluid collects in the tissues of the lungs, trunk, or extremities due to heart disease; it results in difficulty breathing and increased blood pressure; too much salt intake contributes to this condition. Corticosteroid: A substance that reduces inflammation; sometimes shortened to steroid; also called glucocorticoid. Hemophilia: Genetic disorder which impairs the blood’s ability to clot. Infusion: Continuous administration of medication through a catheter. Multiple sclerosis: A disease where the immune system eats away at the myelin, the protective sheath that covers the nerves. Parenteral nutrition: Feeding supplied intravenously; also known as intravenous feeding or hyperalimentation. Peripherally inserted central venous catheter, or PICC line: A catheter inserted through veins in the arm or forearm where the distal tip terminates in the superior vena cava, inferior vena cava, or the proximal right atrium; it is an alternative to central venous access device which has a higher rate of infection; also known as peripherally inserted central venous access. Portacath: A catheter inserted through veins in the arm or forearm where the distal tip terminates in the superior vena cava, inferior vena cava, or the proximal right atrium; it is an alternative to central venous access device which has a higher rate of infection; also known as peripherally inserted central venous access. Rheumatoid arthritis: A chronic, or long–lasting, disease that causes disabling inflammation in the joints.TipsServices represented by Q codes may require prior approval by the payer. See HCPCS S codes for home infusion therapies. Check payer policy on the use of S codes.Additional InfoQ codes represent drugs, biologicals, and other medical equipment or services not identified by national Level II codes when codes are needed for Medicare claims processing. short_description: Chemotherapy administration by other than infusion technique only e.g., subcutaneous, intramuscular, push), per visit
lay_term: This code reports the administration of chemotherapy medications by means other than infusion.ExplanationProviders deliver chemotherapy medications in various ways. Besides infusion, patients can receive drug therapy through subcutaneous and intramuscular delivery. For subcutaneous delivery, the provider uses a short needle to deliver chemotherapy by intravenous injection between the skin and muscle layer of the body. This method is helpful when a patient’s platelet count is low, and there is a danger of bleeding. For intramuscular administration of chemotherapy drugs, the provider inserts a large needle that injects chemotherapy drugs directly into the muscle layer. This method is more rapid than oral administration and avoids additional stomach irritation. For this reason, providers favor it when patients need antinausea medications. Delivery of medication quickly and in large quantities given intravenously is known as an IV push or bolus. The provider uses a peripheral intravenous line or a medication line currently in use. He delivers the medication for the push into the intravenous line, typically taking a short time to administer it.TerminologyChemotherapy: Cancer treatment using chemical agents and drugs. Infusion: Continuous administration of medication through a catheter. Peripheral intravenous line: An intravenous line not currently in use but kept useable for the administration of medication or other therapies. Platelet: A cell fragment shaped like a disc that helps in blood clotting.TipsUse Q0085 for chemotherapy the provider gives as a combination of infusion and other modality such as subcutaneous or IV push. short_description: Screening Papanicolaou smear; obtaining, preparing and conveyance of cervical or vaginal smear to laboratory
lay_term: The provider takes a cervical or vaginal specimen for a Pap smear, prepares the specimen, and takes it to the lab. This code applies to patients with no signs, symptoms, or prior history of genital malignancy.ExplanationThe provider inserts a speculum into the vagina to hold its walls open, then uses a flat, flexible instrument to remove cells from the cervix, or neck of the uterus, and vagina. The provider places the cells in a fixative material, stains them, then sends them to a laboratory. In a separately reportable procedure, a technician then examines these cells under a microscope in a laboratory to screen for possible cancers of the female genital tract.TerminologyCervix: A narrow passage that is part of the uterus; the cervix lies just above the vagina or the birth canal. Human papillomavirus: Virus that causes warts on skin and mucous membranes in humans, especially genital warts. Malignancy: Cancerous tissue. Speculum: A tool to hold the boundaries of a body opening to allow the inspection of the structures within.TipsUse Q codes for supplies, such as drugs, biologicals, and medical equipment, as well as services. Q codes represent supplies and services that do not have permanent codes in other sections of HCPCS. Remember that a screening Pap smear literally screens for potential cancerous or precancerous conditions. For a Medicare patient who has a hysterectomy for cancer, subsequent Pap smears are diagnostic, so report them as part of an appropriate E/M code, for example, 99213, Office or outpatient visit for the evaluation and management of an established patient. Check individual payer policies for frequency limitations on screening Pap smears and the codes they accept for the collection of the sample.Read Less

short_description: Wet mounts, including preparations of vaginal, cervical or skin specimens
lay_term: The lab analyst or microbiologist performs a wet mount preparation of a specimen, usually from material collected on a swab or placed directly on a microscope slide.ExplanationThe lab analyst or microbiologist receives a specimen on a microscope slide or on a swab and performs a wet mount by adding a substance such as saline or India ink, depending on the specimen type and what he will examine. The saline wet mount may reveal living parasites, clue cells, or other agents of interest, while the lab may use India ink alone or in combination with other methods to better define cell wall or cellular objects present. Although not limited to testing for a specific condition, clinicians may order the wet mount for a particular reason, such as for a patient with a suspected vaginal infection.TerminologyClue cell: These vaginal epithelial cells densely covered with bacteria are a clue that the patient has bacterial vaginosis. Protozoa: Single–celled organisms that have a nucleus with a membrane, often have a mode of motion, and may be parasitic. Trichomonad: A parasitic protozoan that has an undulating membrane and four flagella, or microscopic whiplike tails, which allow it to swim; trichomonads often infect the urogenital and digestive systems. Wet mount: Method of preparing a fluid specimen by placing it on a slide and covering it with a slip to keep it moist for microscopic examination, rather than dehydrating it for placement in a permanent mounting medium.TipsFor Medicare and Medicaid patients, remember to use Q0111 or Q0112, All potassium hydroxide or KOH preparation. For non–Medicare and Medicaid patients, you'll likely use 87210, Smear, primary source with interpretation; wet mount for infectious agents, e.g., saline, India ink, KOH preps. Note that in cases of KOH done on other tissue, you should use 87220, Tissue examination by KOH slide of samples from skin, hair, or nails for fungi or ectoparasite ova or mites, e.g., scabies.Additional InfoQ codes represent supplies, such as drugs, biologicals, and medical equipment and supplies as well as services. The lab analyst or microbiologist performs a potassium hydroxide (KOH) preparation of a specimen, usually from material collected on a swab or placed directly on a microscope slide.ExplanationThe lab analyst or microbiologist receives a specimen on a microscope slide or on a swab and performs a wet mount by adding KOH. She then examines the sample under a microscopic slide for the presence of yeast cells and fungal hyphae. If the subject of the KOH test is vaginal tissue or fluid, the analyst may also perform a whiff test as part of the KOH test. This is just what it sounds like: after preparing the sample with KOH, the analyst sniffs it to see if a strong fishy odor is present. Such an odor indicates the likely presence of bacterial vaginosis. Although not limited to testing for a specific condition, note that the KOH test is a screening tool to detect the presence of fungus, but it cannot specify which fungus. A fungal culture is necessary for that level of identification.TerminologyHyphae: Branchlike filaments or threads found in fungi. Potassium hydroxide (KOH): A 10 percent solution of KOH is commonly used to help reveal fungal elements such as hyphae, or the fingerlike projections of certain fungi, in pathology specimens. Whiff test: Part of the KOH test performed on vaginal tissue or secretions; the provider sniffs the KOH prepared sample to detect a strong fishy odor, which indicates the presence of bacterial vaginosis.TipsFor Medicare and Medicaid patients, use Q0112 or Q0111 for all potassium hydroxide or KOH preparation. For non–Medicare and Medicaid patients, you'll likely use 87210, Smear, primary source with interpretation; wet mount for infectious agents, e.g., saline, India ink, KOH preps. Note that in cases of KOH done on other tissue, you should use 87220, Tissue examination by KOH slide of samples from skin, hair, or nails for fungi or ectoparasite ova or mites, e.g., scabies.Additional InfoQ codes represent supplies, such as drugs, biologicals, and medical equipment, as well as services. The lab analyst examines a specimen collected using a pinworm paddle or transparent adhesive tape to look for pinworm eggs or adults.ExplanationThe lab analyst processes a specimen, such as a clear adhesive surface pressed to the patient’s anus upon awakening in the morning. The analyst observes the specimen with the naked eye to see adult pinworms and microscopically to look for pinworm eggs, which are transparent and very small. Although not limited to use for a specific condition, clinicians may order this test to aid in the diagnosis of pinworm infection. Pinworm is a parasite, meaning that it lives in or on a host organism and derives nutrients from the host. Specifically, pinworms live in humans’ rectums, exiting the intestine through the anus while the patient sleeps, depositing eggs on the skin around the anus. The eggs can be transmitted to another host on clothing, bedding, or other objects.TipsUse Q codes for supplies, such as drugs, biologicals, and medical equipment, as well as services. The analyst examines a cervical mucus specimen for a characteristic ferning pattern, most often to determine premature rupture of membranes in pregnancy.ExplanationThe analyst processes a specimen that the provider obtains by inserting a dry speculum into the vagina to hold its walls open for specimen collection. The analyst examines this fluid under a microscope for evidence of a ferning pattern. Although not limited to testing for a specific condition, presence of this pattern may indicate amniotic fluid leakage from the amniotic sac. Ferning also appears in cervical mucus as an indicator of the presence of the female sex hormone estrogen, so the fern test can serve as an ovulation predictor.TerminologyAmniotic fluid: The fluid within the amniotic sac that surrounds the fetus and helps to protect it from mechanical injury. Amniotic sac: A bag of fluid inside the uterus where the fetus develops and grows; it is sometimes called the membranes because the sac is made of two membranes called the amnion and the chorion. Cervix: A narrow passage that is part of the uterus; the cervix lies just above the vagina or the birth canal. short_description: Post-coital direct, qualitative examinations of vaginal or cervical mucous
lay_term: The analyst examines the woman's vaginal or cervical mucus to evaluate sperm interaction with the mucus after the woman and her partner have had sex around the time of ovulation.ExplanationThe lab analyst performs the technical lab steps to analyze postcoital fluid and mucus from the vagina, evaluating it for sperm motility on a microscopic slide. The clinician obtains the specimen after a woman monitors for upcoming ovulation and then, once ovulation occurs, has intercourse with her partner. The clinician inserts a vaginal speculum to hold the walls of the vagina open and then aspirates the fluid specimen. The test may use a microscope to check for the presence or absence of sperm and their motility, or movement, in a postcoital specimen. Clinicians may typically order this test to evaluate the ability of sperm to move through the mucus in the female reproductive tract to help diagnose infertility problems.TerminologyAspiration: Removal of fluid, gas, or other material through a tube attached to a suction device, often combined with irrigation, the instillation of fluid to clean a wound or to wash out a cavity such as the abdomen or stomach. Ovulation: The release of a mature egg from the ovary that is then ready to be fertilized by sperm in the uterus. Postcoital: After sex. Speculum: A tool to hold the boundaries of a body opening to allow the inspection of the structures within.TipsUse Q codes for supplies, such as drugs, biologicals, and medical equipment, as well as services. Q codes represent supplies and services that do not have permanent codes in other sections of HCPCS. See also 89300, Semen analysis; presence and motility of sperm including Huhner test, post coital. Clinicians order this test rarely because of the availability of more accurate tests.Read Less

short_description: Injection, ferumoxytol, for treatment of iron deficiency anemia, 1 mg (non-ESRD use)
lay_term: Ferumoxytol replaces iron in the body in patients with chronic kidney disease who have iron deficiency anemia. One unit of this code represents 1 mg of ferumoxytol. Route of administration is injection.ExplanationFerumoxytol replaces iron in patients who have iron deficiency anemia, so it is a member of the iron product drug class. This code represents supply of ferumoxytol given to treat iron deficiency from chronic kidney disease that has not progressed to end stage renal disease, or ESRD. This code represents only the drug, not administration of the drug.TerminologyAnemia: Decrease in the amount of red blood cells, which results in a lack of oxygen in the blood. Chronic kidney disease: A condition of gradual loss of kidney function, described in five stages, with stage 1 being the least severe and stage 5 being end stage renal disease, requiring dialysis or kidney transplant for treatment. Dialysis: The process of purification of blood by using a dialysis machine as a substitute for the normal function of the kidneys, which are paired organs found in the back of the abdomen that filter waste products from the blood and dispose them from the body. End stage renal disease, or ESRD: Term used to define the final stage of kidney failure where a patient is not able to live without dialysis or a transplant because of the complete or nearly complete irreversible loss of renal function; ESRD is also referred to as end stage kidney disease, end stage kidney failure, and end stage renal failure. mg: milligram Transplantation: To transplant, or transfer, tissue or organs from one person to another or from within one location in the body to another.TipsUse Q codes for supplies, such as drugs, biologicals, and medical equipment, as well as services. Q codes represent supplies and services that do not have permanent codes in other sections of HCPCS. Report Q0138 for ferumoxytol administered to patients who are not yet in end stage renal disease. Code Q0139 reports ferumoxytol administration to patients who are in ESRD. This is a generic drug. Brand names for this drug include: Feraheme®. This code represents the supply of the drug. Check coding and individual payer guidelines to determine whether you can also report the administration of the drug.Read Less

short_description: Chlorpromazine hydrochloride, 5 mg, oral, FDA approved prescription anti-emetic, for use as a complete therapeutic substitute for an IV anti-emetic at the time of chemotherapy treatment, not to exceed a 48 hour dosage regimen

Omnigraft® dermal regeneration matrix is similar but the bottom layer is made of bovine collagen and chondroitin. The collagen layer is the framework that encourages the infiltration of the patient’s own cells and blood vessels to the wound site to regenerate, or regrow, the dermal layer of the skin. The outer silicone layer controls fluid loss and guards against infection. The provider eventually removes this outer layer as the wound heals. This code covers each square centimeter of Dermagraft, a skin substitute that providers use for the treatment of chronic diabetic foot ulcers.ExplanationDermagraft is a human dermal skin substitute derived from the neonatal cells of an infant’s foreskin. The manufacture of this product takes place in a laboratory. Technicians implant human fibroblasts, or immature cells that produce connective tissue in the body, onto a synthetic frame absorbable by the body. The fibroblasts multiply to fill the frame. They also secrete components that create a dermal substitute that contains living cells. The product is cryopreserved until ready for use by a provider for the treatment of a diabetic foot ulcer. The provider applies Dermagraft to the wound and covers it with a dressing to keep the Dermagraft in place. The body eventually absorbs the synthetic frame. Repeated applications are possible without the removal of previous applications. Providers may also use this product for burns.TerminologyCryopreserved: To preserve cells and tissues by cooling them to water’s freezing point. The provider applies Graftjacket matrix to the affected area and secures it in place with the help of staples and sutures. Graftjacket® Xpress, a biological product and medical device manufactured from donated human skin, forms collagen scaffolds, or supporting structures, that the recipient’s body incorporates during wound healing, leading to cell attachment and tissue regeneration. The injection also helps heal deep and irregular wounds. The use of Graftjacket® Xpress injection in wounds helps to avoid amputation in some patients. Graftjacket Xpress® is called a flowable soft tissue scaffold, referring to its liquid flowing properties upon reconstitution. The manufacturer provides Graftjacket Xpress® in a particulate, or powdered, state in a prepackaged sterile syringe, along with a kit including a sterile needle, catheter, and syringe adapter. Report this code for each square centimeter of Strattice™, an acellular tissue matrix xenograft that aids in tissue regeneration and healing of wounds.ExplanationThis code describes the supply of Strattice™, an acellular tissue matrix that repairs damaged tissues by replacing them with new cells. Strattice™ also triggers the growth of vascular tissues and promotes the blood supply in the area of the wound. Providers use Strattice™ to repair the abdominal wall, reconstruct breasts, and repair partial and full thickness wounds, pressure ulcers, venous stasis ulcers, and diabetic ulcers, and other nonhealing wounds. Strattice is available in pliable and in firm forms in varied sizes, and its appearance is that of a piece of skin. TerminologyAcellular: Containing no cells. Biological product: A substance manufactured from live organisms and their products. Full thickness: Refers to the first and second layers of the skin, or epidermis and dermis, and may include the third layer, which is the subcutaneous tissue. Partial thickness: Refers to the layers of the skin, the epidermis and part of dermis. Porcine: Material originating from pigs. Ulcer: An open sore on the skin or on a mucous membrane, generally accompanied by loss of tissue and inflammation. Venous stasis ulcers: Ulcers caused by poor venous blood flow, or venous insufficiency, in the legs due to damaged venous valves that cause blood to pool in veins; also called venous leg ulcers. Xenograft: Transplant of a graft from an individual of one species to another individual of a different species.TipsQ codes include drugs, biologicals, and other medical equipment or services not identified by national Level II codes but for which codes are needed for Medicare claims processing. short_description: Amnioexcel, amnioexcel plus or biodexcel, per square centimeter

These allografts are from human amniotic membrane, or the membrane that surrounds a developing baby during pregnancy. Providers harvest the tissue immediately after birth and dehydrate it along with the extracellular matrix, or tissue that surrounds cells and supports them. These tissue grafts serve to regenerate soft tissues and help treat acute as well as chronic wounds, ulcers, and burns. short_description: Hospice or home health care provided in patient's home/residence
lay_term: This code represents the location at which hospice or home health care services are provided. Report this code for a home or residence location.ExplanationHospice care refers to palliative care given to help terminally ill individuals live their remaining days with comfort. A team of trained professionals provides medical, psychological, and spiritual support to a patient and his family members. A hospice care program combines pain control and symptom management with emotional support. Hospice care is usually provided in the patient’s home. It also can be made available at a special hospice residence or other facility. Home health care includes a wide range of medical services provided to patients at their homes for illness or injury. Home health care services are given by licensed and trained professional caregivers. A home health care program may include personal care, homemaking, and medical services. Report this code for hospice or home health care services provided in a home or residence location.TerminologyPalliative therapy: To treat or relieve the symptoms of a condition but not cure the disease or condition; also known as palliation.TipsQ codes include drugs, biologicals, and other medical equipment or services not identified by national Level II codes but for which codes are needed for Medicare claims processing. For Hospice or home health care provided at other location, see codes Q5002 to Q5010. Read Less

Report this code for a nursing long term care facility or a nonskilled nursing facility location.ExplanationHospice care refers to palliative care given to help terminally ill individuals live their remaining days with comfort. A team of trained professionals provides medical, psychological, and spiritual support to a patient and his family members. It also can be made available at a special hospice residence or other facility. This code represents 1 mg of the ustekinumab biosimilar product Imuldosa™ (ustekinumab–srlf). Providers typically administer this medication subcutaneously (under the skin) or intravenously (into a vein) to treat types of plaque psoriasis, psoriatic arthritis, Crohn's disease, and ulcerative colitis.ExplanationThe typical route of administration for ustekinumab–srlf ( Imuldosa™) is subcutaneous (under the skin) or intravenous (into a vein). Providers may use this drug to treat various conditions, such as plaque psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis. Plaque psoriasis is a chronic skin condition characterized by the rapid buildup of skin cells, leading to the formation of red, scaly patches on the skin’s surface. Psoriatic arthritis is an inflammatory joint condition that affects individuals with the skin condition psoriasis. Providers also may use this drug for patients with Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis. These are inflammatory bowel diseases; Crohn’s can affect any part of the gastrointestinal tract, while ulcerative colitis affects the colon and rectum, both causing severe digestive symptoms and potential complications. These conditions result from an abnormal immune response attacking the body’s own tissues. Report this code for each 1 mg of Imuldosa™ (ustekinumab–srlf).Terminologymg: Abbreviation for milligram, 1/1000 of a gram (g); a metric measurement for mass or weight.TipsReport this code only for ustekinumab–srlf ( Imuldosa™), a product biosimilar to ustekinumab (such as Stelara®). This code represents the supply of the drug. Check coding and individual payer guidelines to determine whether you also can report the administration of the drug. If the dose administered is only part of a single–dose container, and the remainder has to be discarded, you may be able to use modifier JW to report the discarded portion. Check payer guidelines.Additional InfoUse Q codes for supplies, such as drugs, biologicals, and medical equipment, as well as services. Q codes represent supplies and services that do not have permanent codes in other sections of the HCPCS Level II code set.Read Less

This code represents 1 mcg of filgrastim–sndz, a granulocyte colony–stimulating factor (G–CSF), administered by subcutaneous (subcu) injection or intravenous (IV) infusion to stimulate the bone marrow to produce granulocytes, white blood cells in the body that fight infection.ExplanationThe standard dosage of filgrastim–sndz us 5 mcg/kg/day by subcu injection, short IV infusion (15 to 30 minutes), or continuous IV infusion for patients receiving myelosuppressive chemotherapy for cancer or induction and/or consolidation chemotherapy for acute myeloid leukemia (AML); 10 mcg/kg/day over a period no longer than 24 hours for patients undergoing bone marrow transplantation; 10 mcg/kg/day by subcu injection at least 4 days prior to leukapheresis for autologous peripheral blood progenitor cell collection and therapy, continued until last collection; 6 mcg/kg subcutaneously twice daily for congenital neutropenia; or 5 mcg/kg subcutaneously daily for cyclic or idiopathic neutropenia. Filgrastim–sndz is supplied as 300 mcg/0.5 mL or 480 mcg/0.8 mL in a single–use prefilled syringes. Providers may prescribe this treatment for patients with the above–mentioned conditions. This product is biologically similar to other products already approved for use in the same conditions. One unit of this code represents 1 mcg of filgrastim–sndz (Zarxio®).TerminologyAutologous: Describes tissue or blood taken from and returned to the same individual. Biosimilar: Refers to a drug that is biologically similar to or interchangeable with an FDA–approved biological product in terms of indications and effectiveness. Bone marrow transplant: A procedure to replace damaged or destroyed bone marrow with healthy bone marrow cells. Congenital: Describes a condition or defect existing from birth. Intravenous (IV) infusion: The administration of medication, fluid, electrolytes, and/or nutrition to a patient through vein access when the patient cannot take these treatments orally or because of the need for an immediate response. Leukapheresis: The separation of white blood cells from blood to make the blood useful for transplant purposes. mcg: The abbreviation for microgram, one–millionth of a gram, a metric unit of measure for mass; the mc in the abbreviation takes the place of the Greek mu symbol in medical communication. Myeloid leukemia: A type of blood cancer that occurs when myeloblasts (immature blood cells in the bone marrow) enter the bloodstream or when the bone marrow (the spongy tissue inside large bones) produces abnormal white blood cells which then overwhelm or replace healthy blood cells and keep the blood from functioning as it should. Myelosuppressive chemotherapy: Treatment for cancer that reduces or suppresses bone marrow activity, resulting in fewer red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets and causing the patient to be more susceptible to infection. Neutropenia: Decreased numbers of neutrophils, the most abundant form of white blood cells in the blood; neutrophils originate from stem cells in the bone marrow, are short–lived, and are essential to the functioning of the immune system. Subcutaneous injection: Administering medications or other liquids below the skin.TipsReport Q5101 only for Zarxio® (filgrastim–sndz); the sndz stands for the manufacturer, Sandoz. One unit of this code represents 10 mg of infliximab–dyyb (Inflectra®), a tumor necrosis factor (TNF) blocker biologically similar to Remicade®, to be given by intravenous infusion to treat Crohn disease, ulcerative colitis, ankylosing spondylitis, rheumatoid arthritis, plaque psoriasis, and psoriatic arthritis.ExplanationDosages of infliximab–dyyb vary depending on the condition being treated, but a typical dosing schedule is 5 mg/kg by intravenous infusion at 0, 2 and 6 weeks, then every 8 weeks. Dosage may be increased if needed, and the drug may be used in combination with other drugs, such as methotrexate. Infliximab–dyyb is supplied as a single–use vial containing 100 mg infliximab–dyyb powder for reconstitution with 10 mL of sterile water for intravenous infusion. Report this code for each unit of infliximab–dyyb administered by intravenous infusion. Crohn disease, ulcerative colitis, ankylosing spondylitis, rheumatoid arthritis, and plaque psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis are autoimmune inflammatory diseases. Crohn and ulcerative colitis affect the colon; ankylosing spondylitis, rheumatoid arthritis, and psoriatic arthritis affect the skeleton, joints, and connective tissues; and plaque psoriasis affects the skin.TerminologyAnkylosing spondylitis: A type of arthritis that affects the bones, joints, tendons, and ligaments of the spine that can lead to bonelike changes in the connective tissues which result in stiffness or fusion (permanent joining) of a joint. Autoimmune response: Response of the immune system against one's own body. Biosimilar: Refers to a drug that is biologically similar to or interchangeable with an FDA–approved biological product in terms of indications and effectiveness. Crohn disease: A type of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), that may affect any part of the gastrointestinal tract, causing inflammation of the lining of the digestive tract; symptoms include abdominal pain, persistent diarrhea, and rectal bleeding. Intravenous (IV) infusion: The administration of medication, fluid, electrolytes, and/or nutrition to a patient through vein access when the patient cannot take these treatments orally or because of the need for an immediate response. kg: Abbreviation for kilogram, a metric measurement for mass or weight equal to just over 2.2 pounds. mg: Abbreviation for milligram, 1/1000 of a gram (g); a metric measurement for mass or weight. mL: Abbreviation for milliliter, a metric measurement for volume; 1 mL equals approximately 0.034 U.S. fluid ounces; previously known as a cubic centimeter (cc). Psoriasis: A chronic skin condition that commonly causes red patches with scales on the skin; it can be accompanied by a form of arthritis, an inflammatory condition of the joints. Rheumatoid arthritis: A chronic, or long–lasting, disease that causes disabling inflammation and deformity in the joints; in this autoimmune connective tissue disease, the body attacks itself. Tumor necrosis factor: A special type of protein that can induce death (necrosis) of tumor cells but that can also cause inflammation or swelling when it mistakes healthy cells for invaders in patients with autoimmune conditions. Ulcerative colitis: A persistent inflammatory condition of the colon and rectum.TipsReport Q5103 only for Inflectra® (infliximab–dyyb). Report Q5104 for 10 mg of biosimilar Renflexis® (infliximab–abda) and Q5109 for 10 mg of Ixifi (infliximab–qbtx). Report J1745 for 10 mg of infliximab, excluding biosimilars. Avsola™ (infliximab–axx) another biosimilar, has not been assigned a code; you may need to report it as an unclassified drug (J3490), an unclassified biologic (J3590), or an antineoplastic drug, not otherwise classified (J9999), depending on the payer’s preferences. short_description: Injection, epoetin alfa-epbx, biosimilar, (retacrit) (for esrd on dialysis), 100 units
lay_term: One unit of this code represents 100 Units of epoetin alfa–epbx (Retacrit®) administered intravenously to treat anemia in patients on dialysis for chronic kidney disease (CKD).ExplanationEpoetin alfa–epbx, an erythropoiesis–stimulating agent, is biologically similar to epoetin alfa (Epogen® and Procrit®). It promotes the production of red blood cells and helps eliminate the need for allogeneic red blood cell (RBC) transfusions in certain patients. The standard dosage of epoetin alfa–epbx (Retacrit®) in adults with CKD on dialysis is an initial intravenous dose of 50 to 100 Units/kg 3 times weekly and 50 Units/kg 3 times weekly in pediatric patients. Epoetin alfa–epbx is supplied in single–dose vials as 2,000 Units/mL, 3,000 Units/mL, 4,000 Units/mL, 10,000 Units/mL, and 40,000 Units/mL. Report this code for each 100 units of Retacrit® administered intravenously. Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is a condition of gradual loss of kidney function, described in five stages, with stage 1 being the least severe and stage 5 being an end–stage renal disease, requiring dialysis or kidney transplant for treatment.TerminologyAllogeneic blood transfusion: Transfusion of blood harvested from someone other than the recipient; donor blood must be compatible with the recipient's blood. Biosimilar: Refers to a drug that is biologically similar to or interchangeable with an FDA–approved biological product in terms of indications and effectiveness; biosimilars will usually have 3 to 4 alphabetic characters added to the generic name. Intravenous (IV) infusion: The administration of medication, fluid, electrolytes, and/or nutrition to a patient through vein access when the patient cannot take these treatments orally or because of the need for an immediate response. Intravenous (IV) injection: An injection (instillation of liquid) through a needle into a vein. kg: Abbreviation for kilogram, a metric measurement for mass or weight equal to just over 2.2 pounds. mL: Abbreviation for milliliter, a metric measurement for volume; 1 mL equals approximately 0.034 U.S. fluid ounces; previously known as a cubic centimeter (cc). Radiotherapy: Application of high–frequency radiation to target and destroy cancerous tumors; also known as radiation therapy. Transfusion: A process of adding blood products such as plasma or red blood cells to a patient's own blood intravenously, through a vein.TipsReport this code only for Retacrit™ (epoetin alfa–epbx) to treat anemia in patients on dialysis for chronic kidney disease. For patients with CKD not on dialysis and patients receiving Retacrit™ for other indications, see Q5106. See Q4081 for 100 units of non–biosimilar epoetin alfa for patients with ESRD on dialysis and J0885 for 1000 units of non–biosimilar epoetin alfa fir non–ESRD use. short_description: Injection, epoetin alfa-epbx, biosimilar, (retacrit) (for non-esrd use), 1000 units
lay_term: One unit of this code represents 1000 Units of epoetin alfa–epbx (Retacrit®) administered intravenously to treat anemia in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) who are not on dialysis.ExplanationEpoetin alfa–epbx is an erythropoiesis–stimulating agent, which is biologically similar to epoetin alfa (Epogen® and Procrit®), that promotes the production of red blood cells and helps eliminate the need for allogeneic red blood cell (RBC) transfusions in certain patients. The standard dosage of epoetin alfa–epbx (Retacrit®) in adults with CKD not on dialysis is an initial intravenous dose of 50 to 100 Units/kg 3 times weekly, and 50 Units/kg 3 times weekly in pediatric patients. This code may also be reported for the administration of Retacrit™ (standard dose 100 Units/kg 3 times weekly) to patients with HIV infection receiving zidovudine. It may also be reported when given to patients to reduce the side effects of myelosuppressive chemotherapy when the patient is also receiving concomitant hormonal agents, biologic products, or radiotherapy if the patient will receive at least two more months of chemotherapy (but not in those for whom a cure is anticipated or whose anemia can be treated with a blood transfusion). The standard dose for this indication in adults is 40,000 Units IV weekly or 150 Units/kg 3 times weekly, and 600 Units/kg weekly in children older than 5 years. You may also report this code when the drug is administered to reduce the number of allogeneic red blood cell transfusions in patients undergoing elective, noncardiac, nonvascular surgery who are unwilling or unable to donate autologous blood. The recommended dosage is 300 Units/kg daily for 15 days or 600 Units/kg weekly. This drug is not indicated for patients undergoing cardiac or vascular surgery. Epoetin alfa–epbx is supplied in single–dose vials as 2,000 Units/mL, 3,000 Units/mL, 4,000 Units/mL, 10,000 Units/mL, and 40,000 Units/mL. Report this code for each 1000 Units of Retacrit® administered intravenously. Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is a condition of the gradual loss of kidney function, described in five stages, with stage 1 being the least severe and stage 5 being end–stage renal disease, requiring dialysis or kidney transplant for treatment. Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection is an infection of the virus responsible for destroying the immune system in acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS), which can lead to opportunistic infections and malignancies (cancers). lay_term: This code represents the supply of florbetaben f18, a diagnostic radiopharmaceutical used for positron emission tomography (PET) scans, diagnostic nuclear imaging studies, in quantities up to 8.1 millicuries (mCi), depending on the dose needed per study.ExplanationFlorbetaben f18 is a radioactive agent combined with a pharmaceutical used in PET scans to detect the presence of amyloid protein, an abnormal protein that builds up around damaged neurons in the brain, thought to be responsible for Alzheimer’s disease and other cognitive disorders in adult patients. This code reports the dose needed per study, up to 8.1 mCi. PET scans produce three–dimensional images of functional processes in the body; the system detects pairs of gamma rays emitted indirectly by a positron–emitting radionuclide or tracer, in this case florbetaben f18, which is introduced into the body on a biologically active molecule (glucose).TerminologymCi: Millicurie, one thousandth of a Curie, the unit of measure for radioactivity. Neurons: Specialized cells that carry nerve impulses throughout the body. Radiopharmaceutical: A combination of a radioactive compound with a pharmaceutical compound used to identify and treat certain diseases or analyze the function of a part of human body under investigation. short_description: Injection, buprenorphine extended-release (sublocade), less than or equal to 100 mg
lay_term: One unit of this code represents 100 mg or less of extended–release buprenorphine (Sublocade™) administered as a monthly subcutaneous injection in the abdomen to treat moderate to severe opioid use disorder.ExplanationThe recommended initial dose of buprenorphine is 300 mg in each of the first two months followed by maintenance doses of 100 mg each month. The maintenance dose may be increased to 300 mg monthly if the benefits outweigh the risks. The dose may be titrated or incrementally adjusted for patients previously receiving transmucosal buprenorphine–containing drugs. Buprenorphine is supplied as 100 mg/0.5 mL and 300 mg/1.5 mL in a prefilled syringe with a 19 gauge, 5/8–inch needle. Report this code for each unit of 100 mg or less of extended–release buprenorphine administered by subcutaneous injection in the abdomen. Opioid use disorder refers to a pattern of opioid use that leads to clinically significant impairment or distress characterized by a patient’s craving for opioids, extended use of opioids, an increase in or inability to reduce the amount necessary to relieve pain, increased tolerance to opioids, opioid use that interferes with the patient’s ability to function occupationally and socially, and patient’s engagement in physically hazardous situations. The drug may also be prescribed for patients going through withdrawal or taking other substances to avoid withdrawal symptoms. The drug is to be used along with counseling and psychosocial support.TerminologyBuccal: Pertaining to the inside of the cheeks. Subcutaneous injection: Administering medications or other liquids below the skin. Sublingual: Under the tongue. Transmucosal route: A method of drug delivery through the mucous membrane, the moist lining of the nose, mouth, eyes, vagina, and rectum; transmucosal drug delivery can include aerosol inhalation, liquids, quick–dissolving sublingual tablets or film placed below the tongue, and even film placed in the cheek.TipsThis code represents the supply of the drug. This code represents 1 mg of ustekinumab–ttwe (brand name Pyzchiva®). This medication is administered subcutaneously (under the skin) to treat types of plaque psoriasis, psoriatic arthritis, Crohn’s disease, and ulcerative colitis, which are all autoimmune conditions.Explanation The route of administration for ustekinumab–ttwe (brand name Pyzchiva®) is subcutaneous (under the skin). Providers may use this drug to treat various conditions, such as plaque psoriasis, psoriatic arthritis, Crohn’s disease, and ulcerative colitis. Plaque psoriasis is a chronic skin condition characterized by the rapid buildup of skin cells, leading to the formation of red, scaly patches on the skin’s surface.?Psoriatic arthritis is an inflammatory joint condition that affects individuals with the skin condition psoriasis. Crohn’s disease is a type of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) that causes inflammation in the digestive tract. Ulcerative colitis is another form of IBD that causes inflammation and ulcers in the inner lining of the large intestine (colon) and rectum. Report this code for each 1 mg of ustekinumab–ttwe (brand name Pyzchiva®). Terminology Autoimmune disease: Disease caused by the reaction of antibodies against the body’s own proteins.? mg: Abbreviation for milligram, 1/1000 of a gram (g); a metric measurement for mass or weight.? Subcutaneous injection: Injecting small amounts of medications or other liquids in the fatty layer below the skin, sometimes shortened to subcu injection. Tips Report this code only for ustekinumab–ttwe (brand name Pyzchiva®) designed for subcutaneous use. This code represents the supply of the drug. Check coding and individual payer guidelines to determine whether you also can report the administration of the drug. If the dose administered is only part of a single–dose container, and the remainder has to be discarded, you may be able to use modifier JW to report the discarded portion. Check payer guidelines.
